title: Resource Hints: preload, prefetch, modulepreload, dns-prefetch
prerequisites: Understanding of HTML parsing and network requests

progressiveExplaining.eli5: A restaurant kitchen knows some ingredients will definitely be needed for tonight's main dish (preload: fetch them now, don't wait until the cook asks). Some ingredients are likely needed for a later course (prefetch: get them quietly during a slow moment). The chef's assistant also warms up the phone line to the fish supplier in advance (dns-prefetch) so that when an order is placed, the line is already open. Each hint is a different kind of preparation, timed to use spare capacity without disturbing the current course.
progressiveExplaining.junior: Resource hints tell the browser about future needs: <link rel="preload" href="font.woff2" as="font"> fetches a critical resource early (before the parser discovers it). <link rel="prefetch" href="/next-page.js"> fetches a likely-next resource at low priority during idle. <link rel="modulepreload" href="module.js"> fetches + prepares an ES module. <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="//api.example.com"> resolves the DNS early. <link rel="preconnect" href="//cdn.example.com"> opens the connection early. Use preload for above-the-fold critical resources, prefetch for probable future navigations, and preconnect/dns-prefetch for third-party origins.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, resource hints change the resource-loading scheduler's behavior: preload is a high-priority fetch initiated during HTML parsing (before the resource is referenced), reducing discovery latency; prefetch is a low-priority, idle-time fetch cached for future use (in the HTTP cache, not executed); modulepreload fetches a module and parses/compiles it ahead of import; dns-prefetch only resolves DNS; preconnect performs DNS + TCP + TLS handshake. Each has a distinct cost and priority. Overusing preload wastes bandwidth and can starve critical resources; prefetching too eagerly wastes data. The hints must be matched to actual resource timing needs — preload is for resources the CURRENT page needs sooner than the parser would find them.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: The HTML parser, upon seeing a preload link, calls the resource fetcher with a high priority and an 'as' type (font/script/style/image) used for correct request headers (e.g. crossorigin for fonts). Prefetch uses the idle-net stack priority and stores the response in the cache (or memory cache) for later use — it does not execute. modulepreload fetches the module, parses it, and may compile it, so a later dynamic import finds it ready. dns-prefetch triggers an async host resolution; preconnect opens the socket and can reuse it for the first real request. Browsers apply heuristics: Chrome may auto-preconnect to origins discovered via link headers. The hints compose with the browser's priority classes (High/Medium/Low) and the HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection pool.

rosettaStone.react: Vite/webpack emit preload/modulepreload for code-split chunks; React Router prefetch integrations use prefetch hints.
rosettaStone.angular: Angular SSR emits preload for critical CSS/fonts; lazy chunks get modulepreload.
rosettaStone.vue: Nuxt emits prefetch/preload for route chunks and fonts automatically.
rosettaStone.svelte: SvelteKit emits preload hints for critical assets and prefetch for link hover via its own hinting.

codeComparison.title: Font discovered late by CSS vs preloaded font
codeComparison.summary: A font referenced only in CSS is discovered after CSSOM parsing — delaying text render; preloading it starts the fetch during HTML parsing.

legacyOrBad.label: Font discovered via CSS
legacyOrBad.snippet: @font-face { src: url('/fonts/body.woff2'); } /* ❌ OLD: font found only when CSS is parsed */

modernOrGood.label: Preloaded font
modernOrGood.snippet: <link rel="preload" href="/fonts/body.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin /> <!-- ✅ NEW -->

fullFile.code:
<!doctype html>
<html>
  <head>
    <!-- ✅ NEW: The preload hint starts the font fetch during HTML
         parsing, before the stylesheet is even reached. By the time
         CSSOM parsing discovers the @font-face, the font is already
         downloading (or cached). -->
    <link
      rel="preload"
      href="/fonts/body.woff2"
      as="font"
      type="font/woff2"
      crossorigin
    /> <!-- ✅ NEW: crossorigin required for fonts (anonymous CORS) -->

    <!-- ✅ NEW: preconnect to a third-party origin whose first request
         is on the critical path -->
    <link rel="preconnect" href="https://cdn.example.com" />

    <link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles.css" />
  </head>
  <body>...</body>
</html>

interviewGotchas.question: What is the difference between preload and prefetch, and what happens to a prefetched resource?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the resource-hint semantics — interviewers want the priority/execution distinction and the cache behavior, since mixing them up causes real performance mistakes.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: preload is for resources the CURRENT page needs but that the parser would discover too late (critical fonts, hero images, early scripts). It is a high-priority fetch initiated during parsing, and the response is used by the current page. prefetch is for resources a FUTURE page will likely need (next route's JS/CSS/images). It is a low-priority, idle-time fetch stored in the HTTP cache — the prefetched response is NOT executed or rendered, just cached, so a later navigation can reuse it. Key distinctions: preload has high priority and is consumed now; prefetch has low priority and is cached for later. Prefetching too aggressively wastes bandwidth/data, and prefetch does not guarantee the future page will use the exact URL.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'prefetch is just a lower-priority preload'. They serve different pages (current vs future) and have different cache/execution semantics. Another trap: forgetting crossorigin on font preloads — fonts are fetched with CORS mode, so a preload without crossorigin and the actual font request with it are treated as two different requests, wasting the preload. Candidates who explain the current-vs-future distinction and the crossorigin gotcha show real understanding.

interviewGotchas.question: How does modulepreload differ from preload for scripts, and why do bundlers emit it for code-split chunks?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This probes the ES module preparation pipeline — interviewers want to know that modulepreload fetches AND parses/compiles, which is more than preload, and why it matters for dynamic import latency.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: A plain preload with as=script only fetches the file. modulepreload additionally fetches, parses, and (optionally) compiles the module, so that when a dynamic import() or static import later references it, the module is already parsed and compiled — avoiding the parse/compile latency on the critical path. Bundlers (Vite/webpack/Rollup) emit modulepreload links for code-split chunks precisely because navigation or interaction will import them soon; the hint hides the module preparation cost. It also pre-emptively populates the module map. The cost is that parse/compile is real work done even if the module is never used, so modulepreload should target chunks that are likely to be imported.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'modulepreload is preload for ES modules'. It is preload PLUS parse/compile — more work, more memory. Another trap: thinking modulepreload guarantees the module executes — it does not; it prepares it for a later import. Candidates who mention the module map and the parse/compile step show real understanding.
